report:
## Conclusion

The claim that eating dark chocolate lowers stroke risk is **partially supported but overstated**. Here is what the evidence shows:

**Observational evidence is suggestive but not conclusive.** Several meta-analyses of prospective studies have found an inverse association between chocolate consumption and stroke risk. A meta-analysis of five studies (4,260 stroke cases) found a 19% lower stroke risk among the highest chocolate consumers compared to non-consumers ([Karolinska Institutet](https://news.ki.se/eating-milk-chocolate-may-lower-risk-of-getting-a-stroke)). A 2012 prospective cohort study in *Neurology* similarly found lower stroke risk with higher chocolate intake in men ([Neurology](https://www.neurology.org/doi/10.1212/WNL.0b013e31826aacfa)).

**However, evidence quality is low.** A 2019 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis concluded that while chocolate "could have a small inverse association with CHD and stroke," the credibility of evidence was rated "very low or low," highlighting "important uncertainty" ([Springer – European Journal of Nutrition](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00394-019-01914-9)).

**The largest randomized trial did not confirm a significant effect.** The COSMOS trial (~21,000 adults, 3.6 years) found a 10% reduction in total cardiovascular events with cocoa extract supplementation, but this was **not statistically significant**. CVD death fell by 27%, but stroke-specific outcomes were not significantly reduced ([PubMed / COSMOS](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35294962/)).

**Additional caveats:** Most studies do not distinguish dark from milk chocolate, and chocolate is high in sugar and calories. The FDA granted only a *qualified* health claim for cocoa flavanols, noting "very limited scientific evidence" ([FDA](https://www.fda.gov/food/hfp-constituent-updates/fda-announces-qualified-health-claim-cocoa-flavanols-high-flavanol-cocoa-powder-and-reduced-risk)).

**Bottom line:** Observational data suggest a modest association between chocolate consumption and lower stroke risk, but causality is unproven and evidence quality is low. Dark chocolate in moderation may offer cardiovascular benefits, but it should not be relied upon as a stroke-prevention strategy.
